title: The Quebec Bridge Rises Again: AI Agent Recreates Engineering Wonder
summary: See how AI-guided workflows and MicroStation forge faster bridge design, using the Quebec Bridge as a test bed for safe, executable drafting.
body_text: Louis-Martin Losier has given this tour many times. When visitors come to Quebec City, he walks them from the historic Château Frontenac hotel to the Plains of Abraham battlefield, then heads down to the Quebec Bridge, which crosses the St. Lawrence River west of the city. “I tell them, this huge bridge was a great engineering achievement and people called it ‘The 8th Wonder of the World,’” he says. The bridge is just a 13-minute drive from the Bentley Systems office, where Losier serves as a senior product manager for MicroStation, the trusted design platform engineers around the world have used to lay out roads, bridges, and railways for the better part of four decades. The Quebec Bridge earned its wonder-of-the-world reputation the hard way. Nearly a kilometer long (0.62 miles), with a main span of 549 meters (1,800 feet), the steel structure took 17 years to complete. It remains the longest clear-span cantilever bridge in the world. Seven years after construction began, the original bridge collapsed into the river after lead engineers lengthened the central span without redoing their structural calculations. The extra weight buckled the superstructure, taking about 75 workers down with it. And in 1916, with the rebuild almost complete, the new center span fell during hoisting, killing 13 more workers. (The tragedies inspire some newly minted Canadian engineers to receive an Iron Ring, as a reminder “of the tragic cost of human error in engineering work.” The ring is worn on the pinky of the dominant hand, which means that every time they sign a document with a pen, the ring clinks against the table and calls attention to the significance of the act.) Losier recently built the bridge again. Not with 66,000 tons of steel, but as a 3D geometric model inside MicroStation, the Bentley Systems software behind much of the world’s infrastructure. Nor did he build it with his own hands. Instead, he directed an AI agent in plain English, and it controlled the software to create the model. The goal was not a rivet-by-rivet digital replica, but a geometrically faithful, engineering-scale reconstruction that could test how far an AI-driven workflow could go when given the right context, constraints, and tools. A 3D model of the historic Quebec Bridge, which crosses the St. Lawrence River west of the city. An irresistible dare The idea began as a dare. In March, at the 2026 AI in Architecture, Engineering, and Construction conference in Helsinki, Finland, Losier got into a conversation with another attendee about how far the technology could be pushed. The tool they had in mind was Bentley’s Python assistant, released in 2025, an AI aide inside MicroStation that turns plain-language requests into the Python scripts the software can run to build geometry on screen. “He said, ‘It would be cool to use the Python assistant with a complex engineering benchmark,'” Losier recalls. “Then he said, ‘What about the Eiffel Tower?’” Back home in Quebec, Losier gave it a try. The result in MicroStation was crude, for sure, but unmistakably Eiffel-ish. It fired up his curiosity. A plausible tower conjured from a single sentence was a party trick. A giant local landmark that took three tries to build would be a real test. “We needed to find complex benchmarks for our new AI tools,” he says. “If we can achieve high accuracy, we can demonstrate for our users how they can do it, too.” For the bridge, Losier turned to something newer and still limited to Bentley’s trusted testers: the MicroStation MCP server. MCP, short for Model Context Protocol, is an open standard that lets AI assistants operate other software. Bentley’s server is what gives an AI assistant access inside MicroStation. An engineer picks the assistant they already use, such as GitHub Copilot or Claude, and connects it to MicroStation through the server. Everything runs locally on the engineer’s machine, where the server passes instructions from the assistant to a live MicroStation session. Losier supplied the AI assistant with context materials – historical drawings and engineering schematics, dimensions, geolocation data, and modern-day photographs – and told it to create a geometrically accurate model of the bridge. The agent interpreted that intent, extracted what it needed from the materials, and got to work inside MicroStation. His earliest experiments relied on a single, carefully structured prompt that specified the bridge’s proportions, coordinate system, segmentation, and modeling sequence. The results were promising, but they also revealed the limits of trying to capture such a complex engineering process in a single instruction. Nearly a kilometer long (0.62 miles), with a main span of 549 meters (1,800 feet), the Quebec Bridge took 17 years to complete. It remains the longest clear-span cantilever bridge in the world. If at first you don’t succeed “The agent’s first attempts were a bit of a mess,” Losier admits. “The agent confused the profile of the cantilever bridge with Quebec’s Pierre-Laporte suspension bridge, which runs parallel to it nearby, and began blending the two bridge styles.” The trusses also came out wrong. The Quebec Bridge is defined by its eye-grabbing K-truss configuration – a century later, it still gives the bridge an otherworldly look fit for a Ridley Scott movie – but the agent repeatedly reached for more conventional patterns instead. Then there was the ground itself. The early model wasn’t properly georeferenced, floating free of any real-world coordinate system. In subtler forms, that problem is one of the industry’s most common and costly mistakes, says Losier, who has a master’s degree in geomatics, the science of gathering, processing, and analyzing geospatial data. “It was clear the agent had creative capability,” says Losier. “What it lacked was engineering discipline.” So Losier stopped treating the agent like a genie and started treating it like a talented drafting assistant that needed a detailed plan and human oversight. (He had proved the approach once already, on a reconstruction of the Antikythera mechanism, the 2,000-year-old Greek astronomical calculator.) Everything would rest on creating a detailed, structured plan. Losier had an AI agent build it around a set of written specifications that fixed the bridge’s geometry and locked key measurements, forbidding the model from inventing them, which significantly reduced hallucinations. The plan also defined the coordinate system, structural layout, proportions, and construction sequence. Just as importantly, it told the AI how to work. Building a Bridge, One Step at a time Rather than building the entire bridge at once, the plan broke the task into small stages. Losier reviewed and approved each step before the next began. “I told the AI assistant, I don’t want you to create one script that does everything in two seconds,” he says. “I want it built in small chunks of work that can be validated, that we can examine visually on screen, so we catch any errors early instead of letting them compound.” With the detailed plan locked down, he gave it to an AI agent connected to MicroStation through Bentley’s MCP server. Sure enough, the bridge rose section by section, following the sequence laid out in the plan. Constrained this way, the agent behaved beautifully, Losier says. “As long as you define the limits, give clear instructions – use exactly this information, do not hallucinate – you’re giving guardrails, and the agent can do a pretty good job,” he says. The finished model closely matched the real-world geometry of the bridge. Losier was pleasantly surprised by the accuracy of the geometry and geopositioning. “I’m no bridge expert, but I was able to recreate that bridge, with just a few days of effort,” he says. Geometry? Check. Gravity? Check. An impressive drawing and a sound structure are not always the same thing, as the history of the Quebec Bridge demonstrates. Structural validation is the job of Bentley’s analysis software, STAAD, and wiring it into the AI workflow was the obvious next step for Losier. In the future, he says, “I see engineers creating drafts faster with our MicroStation MCP, then using our new STAAD MCP to validate the structural part, before sending the design back to MicroStation for completion.” At this stage, however, his bridge model had the required geometry, but it didn’t contain all the information needed for structural analysis. So Losier went back to the workflow. To sharpen the agent’s reasoning about the bridge’s structural behaviour, he worked with two frontier AI models – Claude’s Fable and OpenAI’s GPT 5.6 Sol – to build a set of specialized skills that drew on photographs, the bridge’s profile, and other characteristics, along with lessons from the previous failed attempts. This enabled him to refine the build plan and tighten the constraints the bridge-building agent was allowed to operate within. This helped the AI better distinguish between geometry that merely looked right and geometry that could support meaningful structural analysis – and ultimately a bridge that could serve people. Losier used an AI agent to run a structural analysis of the Quebec Bridge using STAAD MCP server. With these steps completed, Losier brought in Bentley’s new STAAD MCP server, and he used the agent to run a structural analysis. “What impressed me was that the agent was able to connect the geometric model to a structural analysis workflow,” Losier says. “Engineers will interpret and review the results and adjust the model based on their judgement. These adjustments could be dictated by the engineers to the agent to complete. That’s the kind of iterative loop engineers go through every day. Seeing an agent participate in that process was a glimpse of the future.” Christos Aloupis, a STAAD expert in Bentley’s structural engineering group says that “structural analysis would show the behavior of the structure under different loading conditions, and would help engineers identify potential flaws of the model that might not be easily visible on the MicroStation model. This is also the reason why having the model transferred to STAAD is important.” What Engineers Do Next Losier is careful not to oversell the result. The model is not a perfect digital replica of the Québec Bridge. It captures the bridge’s overall geometry, proportions, location, and primary structural systems, but it does not reproduce every detail of the original structure. Bridge features such as individual connections, hollow multi-layer box chords, and the dense lattice bracing would require a much higher level of detail. “In engineering terms, this is closer to a conceptual or LOD2-style reconstruction than a fabrication model,” says Losier. “The goal wasn’t to reproduce every rivet. The goal was to create and validate a draft model of the bridge’s essential geometry, carry it into structural analysis, and do it in a way that engineers could review, discuss, and improve the design.” And the engineers remain paramount, says Losier: “This initiative is not about replacing engineers. Our goal is to empower them by automating repetitive, low-value tasks so they can spend more time on engineering, innovation, and problem solving.” This workflow is early and experimental, but when it matures, Losier reckons it will change the shape of engineering design. “I see this as a disruptive technology,” he says. “For example, if the agent shows you a draft of the bridge that you asked for, but you’re not happy with it, you can say, ‘let’s change that part,’ and a few minutes later you have a revised design that can be checked again.” That process shifts what an engineer does with their day: less time manipulating complex software, more time exploring alternatives, testing ideas, and deciding which solution is best. The final call, though, is always the engineer’s. “AI can help generate options and accelerate workflows, but accountability and final approval remain with qualified engineers,” Losier says. “The technology will multiply what they can achieve.” Combining AI agents with capable engineering software will have another knock-on effect, says Losier. “A junior engineer who doesn’t yet know the power of MicroStation – the workflows, the tools, and where they sit in the software’s menu ribbon – could start using MicroStation with Claude Desktop or GitHub Copilot, just give their intent, and see results very quickly.” The Quebec Bridge itself is a useful measure of how much has changed. When the last rivets were driven in 1917, some 30 years after the bridge was first proposed, the London journal The Engineer hailed it as “one of the greatest, if not the greatest, feats of bridge engineering the world has ever seen.” More than a century later, one curious product manager, working with modern engineering software and AI, was able to reconstruct its geometry, prepare it for structural analysis, and explore design alternatives in a matter of days. The bridge’s first designers sent 75 men into the river because, when the span was lengthened, nobody redid the calculations. When a change to a complex design can be modeled and re-checked in an afternoon, such corner-cutting will be banished to the past. FAQ: How did the MicroStation MCP server help recreate the Quebec Bridge model? The Model Context Protocol server acted as an open-standard bridge that allowed an external AI assistant to operate MicroStation software locally. By connecting the AI directly to a live session, the engineer could use natural language to direct the agent, which then extracted data from historical schematics and photos to build the bridge’s geometry section by section. What role does AI play in the structural analysis workflow for infrastructure design? AI agents can connect geometric models to structural analysis programs like STAAD to check engineering viability and interpret data loops. While the AI automates repetitive drafting tasks and accelerates alternative design exploration, accountability remains entirely with human engineers who must validate the results to prevent historical structural errors. Why did the AI agent fail its first attempts to model the bridge accurately? The agent initially lacked engineering discipline and hallucinated details, confusing the Quebec Bridge with a nearby suspension bridge and using standard trusses instead of the specific K-truss pattern. It also failed to georeference the model, leaving it floating without real-world coordinates until the engineer implemented a structured plan with strict geometric guardrails.

title: The Next Generation of Transfer Agency | BNY
summary: Transfer agency is no longer a back-office function. BNY explores how fund servicing is evolving to meet new investor expectations, product complexity, and digital infrastructure.
body_text: Securities Services The Next Generation of Transfer Agency How investor expectations, digital assets and operating complexity are changing fund servicing Christine Waldron Katey Neate alarm 6 minute read calendar_today 24 Jun, 2026 Transfer agency has outgrown its back-office label, no longer defined solely as an operational necessity but increasingly evolving into a more strategic, technology-enabled role. The Next Generation of Transfer Agency The Next Generation of Transfer Agency Please fill out the form below to download the White paper. Download the PDF launch As investor expectations evolve, asset managers need servicing models that deliver the same speed, transparency and ease of use investors experience in other digital services. Investors today want simpler onboarding, more intuitive self-service, better access to information and responsive support when they need it. At the same time, fund structures are growing more complex and tokenization is moving from concept to live infrastructure. Asset managers are under pressure to keep pace with these new dynamics — serve more markets, support more product types and reduce costs — without rebuilding their operating models from scratch. Transfer agency creates the most value when it is part of an integrated servicing model. The managers who approach it this way will be better positioned to grow, serve investors effectively and move into new structures without friction. Key Takeaways The transfer agent is becoming a strategic operating partner. The register is still the foundation but the transfer agent is becoming a strategic, technology-enabled extension of the asset manager. Investor expectations have fundamentally shifted. Investors increasingly want mobile access, faster onboarding, real-time information and the ability to transact outside traditional business hours. Product complexity requires a new kind of servicing partner. As asset managers expand into ETFs, private credit, retail alternatives and tokenized structures, they need a transfer agent capable of supporting each. AI is already delivering practical value. AI is improving transfer agency through automation, faster exception handling, and better fraud detection — without replacing human judgment or strong controls. Tokenization changes the transfer agent's role at the design stage. A tokenized fund still requires core transfer agency capabilities but it also requires blockchain connectivity, on-chain/off-chain reconciliation and smart contract design. The transfer agent needs to be involved from the start. The transfer agent needs to move up the value chain. Asset managers are looking for more than processing capacity; they need a strategic extension of their business that can support investor experience, growth into new markets and the shift toward digital and tokenized fund structures. Katey Neate, Global Head of Investor Solutions Partnering with BNY BNY has developed the infrastructure to issue and service tokenized fund units on public blockchains — combining a digital-native fund and transfer agency platform with authoritative off-chain books and records, while enabling interoperability with the broader digital asset ecosystem. Crucially, this operates within a single, global and scalable servicing model across both traditional and digital TA, with day-one client commitments already in place. The key insight is that tokenization isn’t replacing traditional systems anytime soon — both will coexist, and the real challenge is connecting them seamlessly. For asset managers, this means running traditional funds, tokenized share classes and future digital products from one integrated platform, rather than in silos, while enabling full on-chain asset mobility through fiat and stablecoin subscriptions and redemptions within the BNY ecosystem. BNY’s transfer agency capability bridges this gap — which is increasingly why asset managers are choosing BNY for this work . title: How do you prioritize candidates by score to highlight the best ones on the recruiting dashboard?
summary: See how to prioritize candidates by score to highlight the best ones on Jestor's recruiting dashboard.
body_text: In Jestor , each candidate can receive a hiring priority level — ranging from low to high, or on a custom numeric scale — and candidates with a higher priority automatically show up highlighted on the recruiting dashboard. How prioritization works The recruiting system lets you classify each candidate with a priority field, which can be configured as high and low or even on a 0-to-10 scale, based on the company's preference. The higher the priority assigned, the more qualified the candidate is considered for that role. title: Effective Account-Based Selling Strategies for 2026
summary: Discover practical account-based selling strategies to target key accounts and personalize engagement in 2026.
body_text: Title: Effective Account-Based Selling Strategies for 2026 TL;DR: Six strategies to enhance Account-Based Selling: defining clear accounts, personalizing outreach, utilizing technology, coordinating sales and marketing, measuring impact, and improving iteratively. Effective Account-Based Selling Strategies for 2026 Last updated: July 2026 As B2B sales landscapes grow more complex, account-based selling (ABS) has become integral for targeting high-value accounts. In 2026, using specific ABS techniques will be crucial as companies seek personalized engagement with multiple stakeholders. What are the key strategies for effective account-based selling? Account-Based Selling focuses on treating individual accounts as distinct markets, involving personalized interactions across various stakeholders. For 2026, strategies like identifying and targeting high-value accounts, coordinating between sales and marketing, and using advanced tools are essential to enhance this approach. 1. Define and Prioritize Key Accounts An effective Account-Based Selling (ABS) strategy begins with defining and prioritizing key accounts. Identifying which accounts align with your business goals is crucial for maximizing the impact of your ABS efforts. This step involves a keen understanding of your company’s strategic objectives and how specific accounts can help achieve them. It's about focusing not on the sheer volume of leads but on the quality and strategic value of each account. This focus tailors the approach directly to organizations whose needs and objectives closely match your offerings, setting a strong foundation for successful engagement. Once key accounts have been identified, prioritization based on potential revenue becomes the next step. It’s essential to assess each account’s potential return on investment. Start by analyzing factors such as account size, growth potential, and current engagement levels. By prioritizing accounts that present the highest potential revenue, your team can allocate resources more effectively, optimizing sales efforts and enhancing conversion rates. This targeted approach means working smarter, not harder, by investing time and energy where it’s most likely to yield substantial returns. Utilizing data to understand account needs and decision-makers is the backbone of successful ABS. With robust data, teams can dissect each account’s needs, challenges, and buying behaviors. This analysis goes beyond surface-level insights, diving into firmographic data, past interactions, and market trends. Understanding who the decision-makers are and their pain points ensures that outreach efforts are not just relevant but also engaging. Tools that provide deep insights and actionable data, such as those outlined in our article on Account Scoring: How to Prioritize the Right Accounts in B2B GTM , are invaluable for this purpose. The success of ABS lies in strategic account identification, effective prioritization based on potential value, and the diligent use of data to understand accounts deeply. This systematic approach not only amplifies sales efforts but also strengthens relationships with accounts, fostering long-term partnerships. For more on optimizing sales strategies, consider diving into Account-Based Prospecting: A Practical Guide for B2B Sales Teams (2026) . 2. Personalize Your Outreach Crafting personalized outreach is crucial for successful account-based selling. To effectively engage decision-makers, it is vital to develop custom messaging tailored to the specific stakeholders within each account. Each decision-maker's role and pain points can vary significantly, and personalizing your communication helps ensure your message resonates clearly with their unique needs and objectives. Start by understanding the unique challenges and goals of each account. This approach involves thorough research into the company’s industry trends, current projects, and pressing issues. By identifying these specific factors, your outreach can address relevant concerns, positioning your solution as indispensable. From a decision maker’s perspective, a message that acknowledges their individual challenges and offers a tailored solution will stand out in a crowded inbox. Creating personalized content is another key component. This step requires aligning your messaging with the account's objectives, using language and references that reflect their corporate culture and priorities. For example, if you're reaching out to a tech startup focused on rapid expansion, emphasize scalability and innovation in your communications. This can be achieved by referencing recent developments in their industry or highlighting success stories that align with their strategic goals. More tactics can be found in our Account-Based Prospecting guide for B2B sales teams. Remember, personalization is not just about the individual receiving the message but also about the company as a whole. Account-based selling thrives when you consider both the micro (individual decision-maker) and macro (entire organization) perspectives. In tandem with personalized content, this dual focus can optimize your account-based selling strategy, making your outreach efforts more relevant and impactful. For more insights into reaching specific accounts, visit our Target Account Selling guide . Ditch your expensive CRM subscription Get a custom CRM designed for your workflow at a fraction of the price. Talk to our team to get a fixed quote. Book a call 3. Use Technology for Account Insights Using technology for account insights is crucial for implementing efficient account-based selling (ABS) strategies. Tools that provide account insights and data analytics are fundamental in this process. Solutions like LinkedIn Sales Navigator, Salesforce, and ZoomInfo offer deep insights into target accounts by analyzing buyer behavior, engagement history, and market trends. These tools furnish sales teams with the data required to tailor their outreach, ensuring they connect with the right stakeholders at the right time. Automating data collection is another vital component for generating scalable insights. Automation reduces the administrative burden on sales teams, freeing them to focus on strategic tasks. Tools designed for ABS can automatically gather data from multiple sources, such as CRM systems, marketing platforms, and social media, providing a comprehensive view of each account. This automation ensures that data remains up-to-date, allowing teams to make informed decisions quickly. Integrating technology across sales and marketing efforts further enhances ABS strategies. For instance, utilizing an integrated technology stack enables smooth communication and data sharing between sales and marketing teams. By using platforms that support this integration, teams can align their efforts, ensuring consistent messaging and a united approach to engaging target accounts. With these technological advancements, companies can create a cohesive process that enhances the effectiveness of their account-based selling strategies . Moreover, incorporating signal-based systems, as explored in our Signal-Based Selling: The Complete Guide for 2026 , can amplify the impact of ABS by identifying key changes in target accounts, such as leadership transitions or expansions. By staying alert to these signals, companies can tailor their engagement strategies to attend to the evolving needs and priorities of their target accounts. Using technology for account insights not only streamlines ABS operations but also empowers sales teams to cultivate meaningful, data-driven relationships with high-value accounts. 4. Coordinate Between Sales and Marketing Teams Effective coordination between sales and marketing teams is crucial for a successful account-based selling (ABS) strategy. Ensuring these departments work in harmony can significantly enhance your efforts to target high-value accounts effectively. First and foremost, smooth communication between sales and marketing is essential. Both teams need to be on the same page regarding target accounts, messaging, and goals. Regular meetings and shared communication tools can facilitate this alignment. For instance, using a centralized platform where both teams can update and access account information in real-time can help maintain consistency and prevent misalignment. Emphasizing open channels ensures that any insights or feedback about specific accounts are quickly shared and acted upon. Moreover, developing joint strategies that use the expertise of both sales and marketing teams can lead to more effective campaigns. Marketing can craft account-specific content and nurturing sequences, while sales can use these resources to tailor their outreach. Collaboratively, they can create buyer personas and set account priorities, focusing efforts where they will make the most impact. By sharing responsibilities and insights, teams can ensure that both the broader narrative and the tactical messages resonate deeply with each account. Creating cohesive account-targeted campaigns is another vital component. These campaigns should be meticulously designed to use the strengths of both teams, ensuring a unified approach. By collaborating on campaign planning and execution, sales and marketing can present a consistent and compelling message that addresses the specific needs and challenges of each account. This unified front not only serves to capture the attention of target accounts but also builds trust and demonstrates a thorough understanding of their unique situations. For those looking to deepen their understanding of ABS, exploring resources like Account-Based Prospecting: A Practical Guide for B2B Sales Teams (2026) can provide additional insights into structuring and implementing cohesive strategies. Finally, measuring the effectiveness of these coordinated efforts requires consistent evaluation and optimization. Joint reflections on campaign performance, coupled with data-driven insights, can foster an environment of continuous improvement, ensuring strategies remain agile and effective in the pursuit of closing high-value accounts. 5. Measure and Analyze Impact To effectively measure the impact of your Account-Based Selling (ABS) strategies, it is crucial to define clear Key Performance Indicators (KPIs) and success metrics at the outset. Well-defined KPIs provide the framework needed to assess whether your efforts align with your strategic goals. These could include metrics such as conversion rates, deal sizes, and sales cycle length. Each metric plays a significant role in painting a comprehensive picture of how well your ABS strategies are performing and where adjustments may be necessary. Regularly reviewing performance against these objectives ensures that your team stays on target and can quickly identify areas needing improvement. Establish a consistent cadence for these reviews, whether weekly or monthly, to keep your strategies aligned with your goals. During these sessions, examine trends in customer engagement, the effectiveness of personalized messaging, and the performance of your outreach tactics. Insights derived from these analyses allow teams to make informed decisions about where to allocate resources and how to adapt to shifting market conditions. Incorporating feedback loops into your ABS processes is vital for continuous refinement. Collecting feedback from both internal teams and external clients can yield valuable insights into the nuances of your strategy's effectiveness. For instance, internal sales teams may highlight bottlenecks in the process, while clients can provide insight into how your strategy comes across from their perspective. This information is critical in adapting and refining your approach, ensuring that any necessary changes are data-driven. Account-based strategies thrive when they evolve based on real-world performance data. The more you iterate based on solid feedback and performance analytics, the more effective your ABS efforts will become. For additional insights on effective refinement tactics, you might explore our guide on Account-Based Prospecting: A Practical Guide for B2B Sales Teams (2026) , which discusses these concepts in-depth. 6. Iterate and Improve Tactics An effective account-based selling (ABS) strategy must be iterative and adaptable to yield the best results. This involves learning from each campaign to refine and enhance future tactics. As businesses engage more deeply with ABS, they gather valuable insights from their campaigns that can highlight strengths to build upon and weaknesses to address. By carefully analyzing the outcomes, sales teams can make data-driven decisions that improve targeting and engagement strategies. Adopting an agile mindset is crucial in ABS, allowing teams to pivot strategies as needed. Today, sticking rigidly to a plan without room for adjustments can lead to missed opportunities. Flexibility enables sales and marketing teams to respond promptly to changes in customer behavior or market conditions. By regularly reviewing performance metrics and feedback, teams can quickly apply necessary changes to ensure they remain on the path to success. Staying informed with industry trends is another key aspect of continuously improving ABS tactics. The B2B landscape is constantly evolving, and staying abreast of developments ensures that strategies remain relevant and competitive. By integrating insights from industry reports or attending relevant conferences, teams can incorporate the latest best practices and innovative approaches into their campaigns. Resources like our Signal-Based Selling: The Complete Guide for 2026 can help deepen understanding and application of these trends. Consider a sales team working on an ABS campaign for a tech startup: by evaluating their outreach effectiveness and adjusting their approach based on the latest trends in technology sales, they can enhance engagement with key accounts. Such a proactive approach not only strengthens relationships with existing customers but also opens doors to new opportunities in a dynamic business environment. How Miniloop Supports Account-Based Selling In the congested arena of account-based selling (ABS), Miniloop stands as a significant force, streamlining workflows by handling the mundane yet crucial tasks that often bog down sales teams. This practical approach allows founders and teams to concentrate on strategic decisions rather than the intricacies of execution. By offloading time-consuming activities like lead generation, data scraping, and content drafting to Miniloop, teams can focus on developing personalized strategies that resonate with high-priority accounts. Miniloop's integration capabilities allow it to connect with existing systems, ensuring smooth operational continuity. This integration does not create dependency on external systems, a stark contrast to traditional tools and agencies where clients can easily find themselves locked into particular platforms or service models. Instead, Miniloop offers a system ownership model where founders and teams have full visibility and control over their processes. This empowers users to tweak and refine their strategies instantly without waiting on third-party updates or configurations. Picture an organization navigating the nuances of account-based selling. With Miniloop, they don't just adopt a tool; they build a personalized system that can adapt and evolve as their business needs change. From setting it up to maintaining it, Miniloop provides the structure necessary for effective ABS efforts while ensuring that the system remains under the founder’s full control. This unique offering sets Miniloop apart as it delivers not just a service but a sustainable, owner-operated model that enhances ABS efforts without external dependencies. Who Is Account-Based Selling Right For (And Who Should Pass)? Account-Based Selling (ABS) is particularly suited for B2B companies navigating complex sales cycles. These organizations often deal with decision-making units comprising multiple stakeholders, which necessitates a personalized and strategic approach. ABS focuses on high-fit accounts where customized outreach can significantly influence the buying decision by addressing the needs and concerns of each stakeholder involved. In contrast, ABS is less effective for B2C companies or those with low-commitment sales environments. B2C transactions typically don't involve multiple stakeholders, making the targeted and resource-intensive efforts of ABS unnecessary and inefficient. ABS requires a level of personalization and coordination that is not cost-effective in a market where individual customer relationships do not warrant such attention. For companies evaluating a transition to ABS, several key considerations should be addressed. Firstly, the nature and length of your sales cycle play a critical role. If your sales process involves a significant degree of complexity and high-value deals, ABS can provide a strategic edge. Furthermore, your organization's capacity to use data and technology for account insights and communication must be assessed. Establishing effective channels for data sharing and stakeholder engagement across sales and marketing teams is crucial. If your systems are not equipped for such integration, this transition may require additional technological and procedural adjustments. As B2B companies consider the transition to ABS, it is essential to deliberate these factors to determine alignment with their sales strategy. Using resources like the Account-Based Prospecting guide can help clarify the steps needed for successful implementation. These insights ensure a sound decision-making process, positioning organizations for future growth and success in high-stakes B2B sales. The primary goal of account-based selling (ABS) is to focus sales and marketing efforts on high-value individual accounts that have the potential for significant business impact. This approach involves customizing interactions to meet the specific needs and challenges of each account, fostering deeper relationships and increasing the likelihood of conversion. ABS aims to align sales and marketing teams to work collaboratively, ensuring that all efforts are concentrated on nurturing these prioritized accounts for maximum efficiency and return on investment. How does account-based selling differ from traditional marketing? Account-based selling differs from traditional marketing by targeting specific high-value accounts rather than casting a wide net across a broad audience. Traditional marketing often involves generalized campaigns aimed at reaching as many people as possible, while ABS focuses on personalized strategies that address the unique needs of each target account. This personalized approach helps build stronger relationships with key decision-makers, which can ultimately lead to higher conversion rates and more meaningful long-term business partnerships. Is account-based selling suitable for small businesses? Account-based selling can be highly suitable for small businesses, especially those looking to maximize their resources by focusing on high-value accounts with significant business potential. Small businesses often have limited sales and marketing resources, making it important to target efforts where they are most likely to yield substantial returns. ABS allows small businesses to concentrate their efforts on accounts that align closely with their strategic objectives, enhancing efficiency and effectiveness in securing deals and fostering long-term partnerships. What tools can enhance account-based selling strategies? Various tools can enhance account-based selling strategies by providing data insights, facilitating communication, and tracking engagement. CRM systems, data analytics platforms, and marketing automation software are essential for managing relationships, understanding customer needs, and customizing outreach. Miniloop, for instance, offers a system you own that integrates with your existing processes, providing full visibility and control over your ABS efforts, ensuring that the system stays with you even if you decide to manage it internally. How do you measure the success of account-based selling? The success of account-based selling is measured through several key metrics that evaluate the effectiveness and efficiency of ABS efforts. These include account engagement levels, conversion rates, average deal size, and the return on investment for each account. Tracking the length of the sales cycle and customer retention rates can also provide insights into the effectiveness of ABS strategies. It's important to ensure that measurement aligns with the specific business objectives and goals set for the account-based approach. Can account-based selling be automated? Automation can play a significant role in enhancing account-based selling by streamlining repetitive tasks, managing data, and ensuring consistent communication. Tools that automate parts of the process, such as email outreach scheduling and data analysis, enable sales and marketing teams to focus more on personalized interactions and strategic planning. However, the human touch is still crucial, as building relationships with key decision-makers requires understanding and adapting to nuanced needs that automation alone might not fully address. title: A primer on AI for people in the food industry
body_text: As an AI company, we know that understanding AI can be complicated. Part of what makes it difficult is that AI is not one thing. It's a combination of concepts, technologies and methodologies, with the terms used to describe them often used interchangeably, which doesn't help. If you're evaluating AI for your business, both the opportunities and the risks, or even just trying to make sense of the conversation around it, there are a handful of concepts worth understanding. We will cover these in this article, and lay the groundwork for diving deeper into some AI concepts in future posts. ‍ Large Language Models (LLMs) Let's start with large language models or LLMs. This is the engine powering almost all current AI tools like ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini. The breakthrough behind today's AI happened when researchers discovered that if you train these models on enough data with enough computing power, they become remarkably good at predicting sequences of words. At the risk of oversimplification, that is what today's AI is: a very sophisticated word prediction tool. If you give a model the words "Mary had a little...", an LLM will fill the blank with "lamb" because that's the most common completion of those words within the data used to train the model. Through training, AI models have evolved to follow instructions, answer questions, and work through problems step by step. Almost every AI solution uses these LLMs as their engine. We will be exploring how and why all AI solutions are not the same, even though they run on mostly the same engines, in this article and future ones (spoiler: you can put a Ferrari engine in a Toyota, but it still won't run like an actual Ferrari). ‍ Training data Training data is the information that was fed to an LLM during its development, before you ever use the tool. Today's biggest models have been trained on most of the publicly available internet: Wikipedia, books, news articles, forums, academic papers, and more. This is what gives them their general knowledge. But the internet doesn't contain a company's product catalog, pricing rules, or the way their customers actually write orders, i.e. the information that allows AI tools to become useful to a specific business. Those things need to be shared with the AI through context and memory, two concepts we will cover below. ‍ Chatbots The difference between AI, chatbots and LLMs is one area we see often getting confused. LLMs are the engine. Chatbots are one version of the tools powered by that engine. The most well known chatbots are ChatGPT, powered by OpenAI's GPT models, and Claude, powered by Anthropic's Claude models. In simple terms, chatbots enable users to interact with LLMs through a chat interface and have a back and forth conversation. You can ask a chatbot "what's the best way to manage inventory for perishable goods?" and get a reasonable answer. But you can't hand it 200 incoming orders and expect it to process them into your system. Chatbots are just one type of AI tool, and as we will see, one of the more limited tools when it comes to business use. ‍ Prompts Prompts are instructions given to an LLM. They come in two main forms. When you write something into ChatGPT, for example "write an email to John," this is a user prompt, coming from you, the user, and changing for every new request. The other type are system prompts, which are the instructions that an AI tool uses every time it receives a request. For example, a system prompt could be: "whenever a user requests to write an email, start with a greeting and end with the user's signature." Or in food distribution: "when a customer mentions a product without a SKU number, match it against their order history before checking the general catalog." Prompts are where developing AI tools gets very complex, and where specific industry expertise becomes highly valuable, especially in the food sector. ‍ Context Context is what the AI knows right now, for a specific task. Any information you share with an AI tool becomes context for that conversation or use of the tool. Generic AI tools start with zero context about you or your business every time you open them. Effective specialized AI tools should start every task already connected to a business’ context, including its catalog, customers, and pricing, so that they can perform actions and provide information that is useful for that specific company. How well an AI tool integrates the specific knowledge of a business is what separates a tool that's generically smart from one that actually improves business outcomes. ‍ Memory Context is what the AI knows for a specific task. Memory is what it knows across all tasks, built up over time. Context disappears when the conversation ends. Memory persists. Context is knowing that La Trattoria placed an order today. Memory is knowing that they order 40 cases of San Marzano tomatoes and 6 cases of Tipo 00 flour every Tuesday, that they double their order before long weekends, and what they mean when they say "the usual." Memory is what lets an AI tool get better at working with your business over time. ‍ Learning If training is what an AI learned before you ever used it, context is what it knows right now, and memory is what it retains over time, then learning is how all of these work together to make an AI tool actually get better at its job over time. This doesn't mean the underlying LLM is changing. It means the system around it is accumulating knowledge. Every order it processes, every correction it receives, every customer preference it picks up feeds back into its context and memory, making it more accurate next time. When an agent processes 500 orders from the same customer and starts recognizing that "the San Daniele" always means the Levoni prosciutto, not a generic brand, that's learning. The LLM didn't change. Instead, the system got smarter about the business. The ability for AI to learn and improve over time, including doing this automatically in well designed systems, is what makes AI such a transformational technology. But not every AI tool is designed to learn. Most chatbots don't. Building a system that genuinely improves with use takes deliberate engineering. ‍ Hallucinations Even though AI systems can learn, AI has no underlying understanding of what is true or false. It predicts what text seems like it should come next, and provides that answer with confidence. The problem is that something can sound completely right and still be completely wrong. While newer AI models have gotten better at expressing uncertainty, they can still present incorrect information with confidence, which is called a hallucination. Hallucinations are the core trust and risk issue with AI, and the main reason why the quality of the system built around the LLM matters so much, especially in industries where getting it wrong has real costs. Good systems will have guardrails that reduce the risk of hallucinations to a minimum. ‍ Agents If a chatbot answers questions, an agent actually does the work, bringing together all the concepts mentioned above. The result is you don't ask an agent "how should I process this order?" You give it the order, and it reads it, matches the products to your catalog, checks the pricing, enters it into your ERP, and flags anything it isn't sure about. That’s why it’s more useful to think of agents as something similar to a digital colleague, rather than just a tool, in that agents deliver actual outputs and do real work. Building agents that operate reliably is a very different challenge from building a chatbot that can answer questions. To do this, agents need good prompts, the right context, excellent memory, access to tools, ways to avoid hallucinations, and the ability to learn. In an industry as complex as the food industry that involves so many moving pieces, and where access to some information can still be difficult (including the information that is still mainly in people’s heads), getting agents right is very difficult to do. But, ultimately, AI agents are where companies will see the most value in their business. We hope this brief AI breakdown was useful. Feel free to leave any questions for us in the comments, or reach out to our team if you'd like to learn more about the specifics of using AI in the food industry at contact@getburnt.ai or on www.getburnt.ai .
